note: One question per Stack Check control, in plain buyer language. Ids and names match the KB's data/index.json capabilities. Priority 1 controls are the ones we suggest a business asks about first, 2 next, 3 when it builds or runs its own agents.

c4-1.name: Agent ID
c4-1.ask: Does each AI agent get its own identity that we can tie to an owner, the place it runs and the version in use?
c4-1.why: Without it you cannot tell which agent did what, or who answers for it.

c4-2.name: Credential Brokerage
c4-2.ask: How do your agents get passwords, keys and tokens for other systems, and can we limit, rotate, expire and revoke them without the AI model ever seeing them?
c4-2.why: Secrets that sit in prompts or long-lived keys are the easiest way in for an attacker.

c4-3.name: Delegation (OBO)
c4-3.ask: When an agent acts for one of our staff, does it carry that person's identity and permissions to the systems it touches, and nothing more?
c4-3.why: Otherwise an agent can reach data the person asking could not.

c4-4.name: A2A
c4-4.ask: When your agents talk to other agents, ours or anyone else's, how is each side authenticated and what is each allowed to ask for?
c4-4.why: Agent-to-agent traffic is a new path between systems and needs the same checks as people.

c1-1.name: Agent Local Scopes
c1-1.ask: What can the agent do on the computer or server it runs on, such as read files, run programs or reach the network, and how do we restrict that?
c1-1.why: An agent with full local access can do anything the device can.

c1-2.name: Agent Remote Scopes
c1-2.ask: When the agent connects to our other systems, how do we control exactly which actions it may take in each one?
c1-2.why: Connectors and plug-ins often get broad access by default.

c1-3.name: Human Approval
c1-3.ask: Can we require a named person to approve an agent's action before it happens, see exactly what will be done, and have a refusal or time-out stop it?
c1-3.why: Approval only protects you if it is tied to the exact action and fails safe.

c1-4.name: Agent Provisioning
c1-4.ask: How are agents created, changed and retired, and who must sign off on their permissions and settings?
c1-4.why: Agents nobody remembers creating keep their access long after they are needed.

c2-1.name: Agent Orchestration
c2-1.ask: When an agent runs a multi-step task, how do we see the steps, cancel it part way, and recover safely if a step fails?
c2-1.why: Half-finished tasks can leave records or payments in a bad state.

c2-2.name: Inference
c2-2.ask: Which AI model and version handles our requests, where does it run, how is our data handled and what limits apply?
c2-2.why: Model changes and processing locations affect quality, cost and your privacy obligations.

c2-3.name: Execution Environment
c2-3.ask: Where does the agent's code or tool use actually run, and what network and system access does that environment have?
c2-3.why: The runtime decides what a misbehaving agent can reach.

c2-4.name: Agent In-Session Memory
c2-4.ask: What does the agent remember during a session, who can see it, and when is it cleared?
c2-4.why: Session memory can hold sensitive data from earlier in the conversation.

c2-5.name: Harness
c2-5.ask: What software runs the agent's tools, who maintains it, and how is it kept patched and secure?
c2-5.why: The harness is the code that turns a model's words into real actions.

c2-6.name: Agent Persistent Memory
c2-6.ask: What does the AI keep between sessions, such as chat history or saved memories, where is it stored, and how do we control, export or delete it?
c2-6.why: Long-term memory is a store of business data that needs retention and deletion rules.

c2-7.name: Execution Containment & Kill Switch
c2-7.ask: Is agent activity sandboxed, can we restrict where it connects, and how do we stop a running agent or cut its access straight away?
c2-7.why: When something goes wrong you need a way to stop it in seconds, not hours.

c3-1.name: Model Gateway
c3-1.ask: Can we set which models each user, team or agent may use, with spending caps, rate limits and screening for malicious prompts?
c3-1.why: Without central control, cost and risky prompts are hard to manage.

c3-2.name: Tool Gateway
c3-2.ask: Can we control which tools and internet sites each agent may use, and block dangerous actions before they run?
c3-2.why: Tools are where an agent's words become changes in your systems.

c3-3.name: Data Gateway
c3-3.ask: Can we control what data each agent and user may retrieve, and apply data loss prevention to what goes in and out?
c3-3.why: AI search over shared drives exposes any overshared file.

c3-4.name: A2A Gateway
c3-4.ask: Can we set which agents may talk to which, and check the messages they exchange?
c3-4.why: Uncontrolled agent-to-agent calls can chain together into actions nobody approved.

c5-1.name: HITL
c5-1.ask: How can our staff review and correct the AI's output before it is used or sent?
c5-1.why: Human review is the main control against wrong or harmful output reaching customers.

c5-2.name: Behavioural
c5-2.ask: How do you check that agents keep doing their job properly over time, and alert us to unusual behaviour?
c5-2.why: Agents can drift as models, data and prompts change.

c5-3.name: Cost & Yield
c5-3.ask: What reporting do you give us on usage and cost, so we can see what we spend and what we get for it?
c5-3.why: Token and seat costs grow quietly without reporting.

c5-4.name: Infrastructure
c5-4.ask: What monitoring do you provide for performance, outages and unusual load on the AI service?
c5-4.why: You need to know when the service is degraded before your staff or customers do.

c5-5.name: Connectivity
c5-5.ask: Can we see, in plain terms, every system each agent can reach and what it could do there?
c5-5.why: You cannot judge an agent's risk without knowing its reach.

c7-1.name: Administrative Audit
c7-1.ask: Is every agent action logged with who, what and when, in a record that cannot be altered, or can we export it to storage that cannot be altered?
c7-1.why: Investigations and insurers rely on logs nobody could have edited.

c7-2.name: SOC Telemetry
c7-2.ask: Can we send AI activity and security events to our security monitoring, with users and sessions linked and sensitive content masked?
c7-2.why: Your security team or provider cannot watch what never reaches them.

c7-3.name: Model Assurance
c7-3.ask: What do you publish about where your models come from and how they are checked, such as model cards, lineage or an AI bill of materials?
c7-3.why: Model provenance matters for regulated work and for supply chain risk.

c7-4.name: Runtime Assurance
c7-4.ask: How do you secure and check the servers and containers that run the model and its tools?
c7-4.why: The runtime holds your data while it is processed.

c7-5.name: First-Party Tool Assurance
c7-5.ask: How do you scan and review the tools, connectors and extensions you supply, and do you publish a software bill of materials for them?
c7-5.why: Vendor-built connectors run with access to your data.

c7-6.name: Third-Party Tool Assurance
c7-6.ask: When we add third-party plug-ins, skills or MCP servers, how do you protect us from fake, poisoned or compromised ones?
c7-6.why: Plug-in marketplaces are a known supply chain attack route.

c7-8.name: Data & Feature Stores
c7-8.ask: How is the data your AI retrieves from, such as indexes and knowledge bases, governed, cleaned and secured?
c7-8.why: Poisoned or stale knowledge bases lead to wrong or unsafe answers.

c7-9.name: AI Discovery
c7-9.ask: Can you help us find AI use we did not approve, such as personal accounts or unsanctioned apps?
c7-9.why: Staff often use personal AI accounts with business data.

c7-10.name: Automated AI Pen-Testing
c7-10.ask: Do you support, or carry out, authorised automated attack testing of the AI, its data sources and its tools?
c7-10.why: Prompt injection and tool misuse are found by testing, not by reading policy.

c6-1.name: Asset Registries & Inventory
c6-1.ask: Can we get a list of every model, agent and tool in use in our account, with their versions and components?
c6-1.why: An AI register starts with knowing what you have.

c6-2.name: Registration & Approval Workflows
c6-2.ask: Is there a way to submit and approve new agents, models or tools before staff can use them?
c6-2.why: Approval before use is cheaper than clean-up after.

c6-3.name: Posture & Reporting
c6-3.ask: What reporting shows us which controls are on, where policy is breached and what risks are open?
c6-3.why: Boards and auditors ask for this view.

c6-4.name: Policy Management
c6-4.ask: Can we write, version and publish our AI use policies in the product, and see who owns and reviews each one?
c6-4.why: Policies that live only in a document are hard to apply.

c6-5.name: AI Lifecycle Management
c6-5.ask: How do agents and AI use cases move from trial to live use to retirement, and what checks apply at each stage?
c6-5.why: Pilots tend to become production without a review.

c6-6.name: Ownership & Accountability
c6-6.ask: Can we assign a named owner to each agent, model and tool, and keep that up to date when people change roles?
c6-6.why: Every AI system needs someone who answers for it.

c6-7.name: Risk Assessment & Classification
c6-7.ask: Does the product help us assess each AI use, give it a risk level and pick the right controls?
c6-7.why: Not every use needs the same controls, but you need to know which is which.

c6-8.name: Change & Release Governance
c6-8.ask: How are changes to models, prompts, tools, permissions and knowledge approved, versioned and rolled back?
c6-8.why: A silent model or prompt change can alter results overnight.

c6-9.name: Exceptions & Risk Acceptance
c6-9.ask: Can we record exceptions to our AI policy, who approved them and when they expire?
c6-9.why: Exceptions without an end date become the rule.

c6-10.name: Data Lifecycle Governance
c6-10.ask: How long do you keep our prompts, outputs, files and agent memory, where are they stored, can we choose Australia, and do you use them to train models?
c6-10.why: Retention, location and training use decide most of your privacy obligations.

c6-11.name: Assurance & Compliance Evidence
c6-11.ask: Can we collect evidence that our controls are working, mapped to the requirements and audits we answer to?
c6-11.why: Audits go faster when the evidence is already gathered.

c6-12.name: Third-Party Governance
c6-12.ask: Which other companies, including model providers and sub-processors, handle our data, and how do you approve and review them?
c6-12.why: Your data goes wherever your vendor's suppliers take it.

c6-13.name: Independent Assurance & Authorisation
c6-13.ask: Which independent assessments cover this product, such as IRAP, SOC 2, ISO 27001 or ISO 42001, and what is in scope and when were they done?
c6-13.why: A certificate only helps if it covers the product and features you use.
